interviewQuestions.question: My element has width: 300px but it's rendering wider than 300px on the page. Why?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Almost always this is `box-sizing`. Under the CSS default, `content-box`, the `width` you set only describes the content area — any padding and border you add get added *on top* of that 300px, not carved out of it. A 300px box with 20px padding and a 2px border renders at 344px, not 300px.

My diagnostic order out loud: first I open DevTools' computed box model panel and read the actual content/padding/border numbers rather than guessing from the stylesheet — that tells me in five seconds whether padding is the culprit. Then I check whether a global `box-sizing: border-box` reset is present; if it's missing on this element specifically, that's the fix.

The reason this bug is so common: percentage widths make it worse. `width: 100%; padding: 1rem` under content-box overflows the parent by 2rem, because the 100% and the padding are two separate additive quantities. That's exactly why teams put `*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }` at the very top of their reset — it makes width mean what people intuitively expect it to mean.

It's rarely margin, since margin is outside the border and doesn't affect the element's own rendered width — it just changes where neighbors sit.

**Testing:** whether you reach for the box-sizing explanation first, or start guessing at unrelated properties.

interviewQuestions.question: Why does border-box get recommended as a global default over content-box?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because content-box makes `width` mean something almost nobody wants once padding or a border is involved. With content-box, width sets the content area alone, so padding and border add extra pixels beyond it — meaning a percentage width plus any padding routinely overflows its container. That single interaction produces a large share of real-world unexpected-scrollbar and overflow bugs.

With `border-box`, width sets the outer edge instead: `width: 50%; padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid` renders at exactly 50% of the parent, with padding and border eaten out of that space. This makes width composable with padding and border in the way responsive layouts actually need — you can add a border to a component for a debug outline without it shifting the layout.

The standard fix is the universal reset:
```css
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
```
including pseudo-elements, because a component whose padded `::before` uses content-box while the element itself uses border-box produces a subtly mismatched box that's hard to spot in review.

This is treated industry-wide as a correction to an original CSS spec default that turned out to be the wrong choice, not a matter of taste — it's one of the first rules in nearly every reset stylesheet and CSS framework.

**Testing:** whether you understand this as fixing a specific compounding bug, not just repeating "it's best practice."

interviewQuestions.question: Why did the vertical gap between two stacked divs turn out smaller than the sum of their margins?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
That's margin collapsing, and it only applies to **vertical** margins between block-level boxes in normal flow. When one element's `margin-bottom` meets the next element's `margin-top`, the two don't add — the browser keeps only the larger of the two values as the actual gap.

There are three cases where this shows up: between adjacent siblings, between a parent and its first or last child when nothing separates them (no border, padding, or inline content in between), and even between an empty element's own top and bottom margin collapsing into each other.

A concrete case that surprises people more: a heading's `margin-top` inside an otherwise-empty container can collapse straight through the parent and push the *parent* down, rather than adding space inside it, because the parent has no border or padding to stop the collapse.

The fix, when you don't want it: give the parent any padding, any border, or `overflow: hidden`/`auto` (which establishes a new block formatting context) — any of those stops the collapse. This is also one of the quieter reasons layouts move to flexbox or grid: items inside a flex or grid container never collapse margins with each other, so `gap` gives predictable spacing where margin math was fragile.

**Testing:** whether you know collapsing is a specific, scoped behavior — not just "margins are unpredictable."

interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through debugging a layout where an element's width doesn't match what you set in CSS.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd work through a fixed checklist rather than guess randomly, because this bug has a small number of actual root causes.

First, **box-sizing** — is it content-box (the default, if no reset is applied) with padding or a border present? That alone explains most "wider than I set it" cases, since padding and border add on top of the width instead of being carved out of it.

Second, **what the percentage is resolving against**. A percentage width resolves against the element's *containing block*, which isn't always the visual parent — under `position: absolute` it resolves against the nearest positioned ancestor, which can be several levels up and a different size than expected.

Third, **display type**. An `inline` element silently ignores `width`/`height` altogether; that reads exactly like a box-model bug in the DOM inspector but has nothing to do with box-sizing.

Fourth, I open DevTools' computed box model panel, which shows the actual resolved content/padding/border/margin numbers directly — this settles the first three in seconds instead of trial-and-error edits.

I've been asked this live in interviews specifically because it separates people who've memorized the box model from people who can diagnose with it under time pressure — saying the checklist out loud, in this order, usually matters as much as landing on the right cause.

**Testing:** whether you have a repeatable diagnostic process instead of a single memorized fact.
